title: Credit, Borrowing and Protecting Your Money
bigQuestion: When does borrowing help you, and how can you keep your money safe from high costs and scams?

story.title: Zero Down, Read the Rest
story.kicker: The sign said $0 down. The fine print told a longer story.
paragraphs: Priya walked past a phone store on State Street in Chicago. A bright sign in the window said NEW PHONE, $0 DOWN! Her old phone had a cracked screen. The new one cost $999 in this example. She did not have $999, but $0 sounded perfect.

Inside, a salesperson smiled and slid a tablet across the counter. "Just sign here," he said. "It is only $35 a month." Priya's older cousin Dev was with her. He asked a simple question. "For how many months?"

The answer was on the second page, in small letters. It said 36 months. There was also a $15 activation fee, and she had to keep a $70-a-month phone plan. Dev took out his calculator. $35 times 36 months is $1,260. That was $261 more than the $999 price.

Priya did not sign that day. She went home and made a list of questions. What is the total cost? What happens if I miss a payment? What if I want to leave early? The sign was not a lie, but it was not the whole story. That is why people read the fine print.
story.think: Why would a store advertise $0 down instead of the total price? What questions should you ask before signing?

lessons.title: Credit: Buy Now, Pay Later
lessons.mainIdea: Credit lets you use money now and pay it back later, usually with interest.
reading: *Credit* means borrowing money now and paying it back later. The person or business that lends is the *lender*. The borrower pays back the money borrowed, called the principal. Most lenders also charge interest, the price of using their money.

Here is an example. Jamal borrows $500 from a bank to fix his car so he can get to work. He agrees to pay 10% interest for one year. At the end of the year he owes $500 + $50 = $550. The $50 is the cost of getting the money early.

Credit can help. It lets people buy a home, pay for school or handle a real emergency. It can also hurt. Borrowing for wants can leave you paying for things long after you enjoy them. A common mistake is to think borrowed money is free. It always costs more than paying cash.

words.d: an agreement to get money, goods or services now and pay later
a person or business that lends money
a person who receives a loan and must pay it back

look.title: Worth Borrowing?
look.text: Case 1: Kira borrows to buy a used car so she can get to a better-paying job. Case 2: Tom borrows to buy a big TV for a party.
look.prompt: Which loan is more likely to pay off in the long run? Explain using costs and benefits.

check.q: Jamal borrows $500 at 10% simple interest for one year. How much does he pay back?
What is interest from a borrower's view?
choices: A tax paid to the city
The price paid for using someone else's money
check.why: Borrowers pay interest as the cost of the loan.

check.q: Which is the best reason to borrow?
choices: To pay for training that raises future pay
To buy concert tickets you want
To buy a new phone when yours works fine
check.why: Borrowing makes more sense when it helps you earn more later.

lessons.title: Debit Cards and Credit Cards
lessons.mainIdea: A debit card spends your own money; a credit card spends borrowed money that you must repay.
reading: Two cards can look almost the same. A *debit card* takes money straight out of your bank account. If you have $80 in the account and buy a $30 shirt, $50 is left. You cannot easily spend money you do not have.

A *credit card* is different. Each purchase is a small loan from the card company. At the end of the month you get a bill. If you pay the whole balance by the due date, many cards charge no interest. If you pay only part, interest is added to the rest.

Both cards have benefits. Paying on time with a credit card can build a credit history. Credit cards often have strong fraud protection. The danger is that it is easy to spend more than you earn. A common mistake is to think the minimum payment is all you owe.

words.d: a card that takes money directly from your bank account
a card that lets you borrow money for purchases and pay it back later
the amount of money owed on a card or held in an account

look.title: Same Shirt, Two Cards
look.text: Ella buys a $40 shirt with a debit card. Omar buys the same shirt with a credit card and pays only $10 when the bill comes.
look.prompt: Where did each person's money come from? What happens to Omar's remaining $30?

check.q: You have $120 in your bank account and spend $45 with a debit card. What is left?
check.why: $120 - $45 = $75. Debit takes money right from your account.

check.q: How can you avoid paying interest on most credit cards?
choices: Pay the full balance by the due date
check.why: Many cards charge no interest if the full balance is paid on time.

check.q: Which is true of a credit card?
choices: It spends only money already in your account
It is the same as cash
Each purchase is borrowed money you must repay
check.why: A credit card is a loan. A debit card uses your own money.

lessons.title: APR in Plain Words
lessons.mainIdea: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing shown as a percent, and a higher APR means a more expensive loan.
reading: Loans and credit cards list an *APR*, or annual percentage rate. It is the cost of borrowing for a year, shown as a percent. It can include some fees as well as interest. Comparing APRs is a quick way to see which loan costs less.

Say a credit card has an APR of 24%, an example rate. Divide by 12 months: 24 divided by 12 is 2% a month. If you carry a $1,000 balance, one month of interest is about 2% of $1,000, or $20. Leave it for a year and it adds up to hundreds of dollars.

Now compare two offers for a $1,000 loan for one year. Offer A has an APR of 8%. Offer B has an APR of 20%. Using simple yearly interest, A costs about $80 and B costs about $200. A lower monthly payment can hide a higher APR or a longer loan. Look at both.

words.d: annual percentage rate; the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percent
the smallest amount you must pay on a bill each month to avoid a late fee

look.title: Interest on a $1,000 Balance for One Year (example)
look.cite: Made-up example using simple yearly interest on a $1,000 balance
look.prompt: How much more does the 24% APR cost than the 8% APR?

check.q: A card has an APR of 18%. About what is the monthly rate?
check.why: 18% divided by 12 months = 1.5% a month.

check.q: Which $2,000 loan for one year costs less?
check.why: The lower APR means less interest: 9% of $2,000 is $180.

check.q: A $600 balance on a card with 2% monthly interest is left for one month. About how much interest is added?

lessons.title: What a Credit Score Is
lessons.mainIdea: A credit score is a number that shows lenders how likely you are to repay on time.
reading: Lenders want to know if you will pay them back. So they check your *credit report*. It is a record of your loans and cards and whether you paid on time. Companies called credit bureaus collect this record. You have the right to see your own reports for free.

A *credit score* turns that record into one number. The most widely used scores run from 300 to 850. A higher score tells lenders you are lower risk. People with higher scores often get loans at lower interest rates.

Here is why that matters. Two people borrow $20,000 for a car. One gets an example rate of 5% because of a strong score. The other gets 12%. In the first year alone, that is about $1,000 versus about $2,400 in interest. A good score can save real money.

words.d: a record of a person's borrowing and whether bills were paid on time
a number, often from 300 to 850, that shows how likely a person is to repay debts

look.title: Two Borrowers
look.text: Ben pays every bill on time. Carla has missed several payments. Both ask for the same $10,000 loan.
look.prompt: Which person is likely to get the lower interest rate? Why does the lender care?

check.q: What does a higher credit score usually mean for a borrower?
check.why: Lenders see lower risk, so they charge less.

check.q: What range do the most widely used credit scores cover?
check.why: The most common scores run from 300 to 850.

check.q: A $20,000 loan at 5% versus 12% for one year. About how much more interest at 12%?

lessons.title: What Changes Your Score
lessons.mainIdea: Paying on time and keeping balances low are the biggest ways to build a good credit score.
reading: The company FICO makes the most widely used score. It publishes the rough weight of each part. Payment history, whether you pay on time, counts most, about 35%. How much you owe counts about 30%.

Length of credit history counts about 15%. New credit, meaning recent loan applications, counts about 10%. Credit mix, the kinds of credit you have, counts about 10%. Add them: 35 + 30 + 15 + 10 + 10 = 100.

So the best habits are simple. Pay every bill on time. Keep card balances well below the limit. Say your limit is $1,000 and you owe $900. You are using 90% of your credit, which can lower your score. Owing $200 uses only 20%. A common myth is that checking your own report hurts your score. It does not.

words.d: the record of how long and how well a person has handled credit
the most a lender lets you borrow on a card

look.title: What Goes Into a FICO Score
look.cite: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation), "What's in my FICO Scores?" general weights
look.prompt: Which two parts together make up about two-thirds of the score?

check.q: Which habit helps a credit score the most?
choices: Opening many new cards at once
Using all of your credit limit
check.why: Payment history is the largest part, about 35%.

check.q: Your limit is $2,000 and you owe $500. What percent of your credit are you using?
Does checking your own credit report lower your score?
check.why: Looking at your own report does not hurt your score.

lessons.title: Loans for Big Things
lessons.mainIdea: Big purchases like cars, college and homes often use loans that are repaid in monthly payments over years.
reading: Some things cost too much to pay for all at once. Many people use a *loan* repaid in set monthly payments. Three common kinds are car loans, student loans and mortgages. Each one works a little differently.

A car loan usually lasts a few years. A *student loan* pays for college or training. Payments often start after school ends. A *mortgage* is a loan to buy a home, often over 15 or 30 years. If the borrower stops paying, the lender can take the car or the home. That property is called *collateral*.

Longer loans have smaller payments but cost more in total. Say a loan has payments of $300 a month for 48 months (an example). The total is $300 x 48 = $14,400. Another choice is $250 a month for 72 months. That total is $250 x 72 = $18,000. The lower payment costs $3,600 more.

words.d: money borrowed that must be repaid, usually with interest
a loan used to buy a home, repaid over many years
a loan that pays for college or job training
property a lender can take if a loan is not repaid

look.title: Longer or Shorter?
look.text: Two car loans for the same car: $400 a month for 36 months, or $300 a month for 60 months (example amounts).
look.prompt: Find the total cost of each. Which would you choose, and what is the trade-off?

check.q: A loan is $400 a month for 36 months. What is the total paid?
What is a mortgage?
choices: A loan to buy a home
check.why: A mortgage is a home loan, often lasting 15 or 30 years.

check.q: Why does a longer loan with smaller payments often cost more in total?
choices: The price of the item rises
The bank adds a free month
You pay interest for more months
check.why: More time borrowing means more interest paid in total.

lessons.title: Spotting Scams and Phishing
lessons.mainIdea: Scammers create pressure and ask for private information, so slow down and check before you act.
reading: Mia gets a text: "Your bank account is locked! Click here and enter your password now." It looks real. But it is a *scam*, a trick to steal money or information. This kind, where a fake message fishes for private details, is called *phishing*.

Scams often share warning signs. They rush you: act now or lose out. They ask for passwords, account numbers or a Social Security number. They ask you to pay with gift cards or a money app. They promise prizes you never entered to win.

What helps: stop and do not click. Contact the company yourself using a number or website you already trust. Real banks do not ask for your password by text. Tell a trusted adult. You can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. agency that protects consumers.

words.d: a trick to steal someone's money or personal information
a fake email, text or call that tries to get private information

look.title: Is It Real?
look.text: A message says: "You won a $500 gift card! Pay a $20 shipping fee in gift cards within one hour to claim it."
look.prompt: List every warning sign you can find. What should you do?

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a scam?
choices: A demand to pay right away with gift cards
A receipt from a store where you shopped
A bill for a service you used
A letter you expected from school
check.why: Pressure plus gift-card payment is a common scam sign.

check.q: A text says your bank account is locked and asks for your password. What should you do?
choices: Contact the bank yourself using a number you trust
check.why: Real banks do not ask for passwords by text. Check through a trusted channel.

check.q: What is phishing?
choices: A safe way to pay bills
A fake message that tries to get private information
check.why: Phishing fishes for passwords and account numbers with fake messages.

lessons.title: Guarding Against Identity Theft
lessons.mainIdea: Identity theft is when someone uses your personal information, and simple habits make it much harder.
reading: *Identity theft* happens when someone uses your name, Social Security number or account numbers without permission. A thief might open a credit card in your name. Then you learn about it when the bills or a low credit score show up.

Simple habits help. Use strong, different passwords for important accounts. Turn on two-step login when you can. Do not share your Social Security number unless it is truly needed. Shred papers with account numbers before throwing them away.

Check your bank statements and credit reports. You can get free credit reports from the three national credit bureaus through AnnualCreditReport.com. If something looks wrong, act fast. The FTC's IdentityTheft.gov site gives step-by-step recovery plans. Catching a problem early limits the damage.

words.d: using someone else's personal information without permission, often to steal money
details like your Social Security number, passwords and account numbers

look.title: Something Looks Wrong
look.text: Leah checks her bank statement and sees a $75 charge from a store in another state. She has never been there.
look.prompt: What steps should Leah take, and in what order?

check.q: Which habit best protects against identity theft?
choices: Posting your birthday and address online
Throwing old bank papers in the trash whole
check.why: Different strong passwords mean one leak does not open every account.

check.q: How can you get free credit reports from the national bureaus?
check.why: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site for free reports.

check.q: Why check your bank statement each month?
choices: To catch charges you did not make
check.why: Finding strange charges early limits the damage.

lessons.title: What Insurance Is For
lessons.mainIdea: Insurance lets many people pay small amounts so that no one has to face a huge loss alone.
reading: Imagine 1,000 drivers. Each year, a few of them will have a costly accident. No one knows who. *Insurance* is a deal: each person pays a small, regular amount, called a *premium*. The company uses the pool of money to pay for the few big losses.

Here is an example. Each driver pays $1,200 a year. That is $1.2 million from all 1,000 drivers. If 20 drivers each have a $40,000 accident, claims total $800,000. The pool covers them, plus the company's costs. A *deductible* is the part of a loss you pay yourself before insurance pays. Say it is $500 and the repair costs $3,000. You pay $500 and insurance pays $2,500.

Common kinds are health, car, home or renters, and life insurance. Most states, including Illinois, require car insurance to drive. The trade-off is clear. You pay a sure small cost to avoid a possible large one.

words.d: a plan where people pay regular amounts so a company will cover large losses
the regular amount paid for insurance
the part of a loss you pay yourself before insurance pays the rest

look.title: Renters Insurance
look.text: Sam rents an apartment. Renters insurance costs $15 a month (example). His laptop, bike and clothes are worth about $4,000.
look.prompt: What does Sam pay in a year? Is the trade-off worth it? Why or why not?

check.q: A repair costs $2,000. The deductible is $500. How much does insurance pay?
check.why: Insurance pays the loss minus the deductible: $2,000 - $500 = $1,500.

check.q: What is a premium?
choices: The amount insurance pays after a loss
check.why: You pay the premium to keep the insurance.

check.q: Why does insurance work?
choices: Many people's small payments cover a few people's large losses
check.why: Pooling spreads the risk among many people.

lessons.title: Comparing Prices
lessons.mainIdea: Compare the unit price and the total cost, not just the sticker price or the monthly payment.
reading: At the store, a 12-ounce cereal box costs $3.60 and a 20-ounce box costs $5.00. These are example prices. Which is the better deal? Find the *unit price*, the cost for one unit. $3.60 divided by 12 is $0.30 an ounce. $5.00 divided by 20 is $0.25 an ounce. The bigger box costs less per ounce.
The same idea works for bigger buys. Go back to Priya's phone. Paying $999 at once is cheaper than $35 a month for 36 months, which is $1,260. The *total cost* includes every payment and every fee.

A bigger box is only a better deal if you will use it before it spoils. A sale is only a savings if you meant to buy the item anyway. Comparing prices is about value for you, not just the lowest number.

words.d: the cost for one unit, such as one ounce or one item
the full amount paid, including all payments, interest and fees

look.title: Cereal Unit Prices (example)
look.prompt: Which box has the lowest unit price? Why might someone still buy another box?

check.q: A 10-ounce bag costs $2.50. What is the unit price?
check.why: $2.50 divided by 10 ounces = $0.25 an ounce.

check.q: A phone is $50 a month for 24 months plus a $30 fee. What is the total cost?
Which is the best way to compare two sizes of the same item?
choices: Pick the bigger box every time
check.why: Unit price shows the cost per ounce, so different sizes can be compared fairly.

lessons.title: Reading a Contract
lessons.mainIdea: A contract is a promise that the law can enforce, so read it and ask questions before you sign.
reading: A *contract* is an agreement between two or more people that the law can enforce. A phone plan, a loan or an apartment lease is a contract. Once you sign, you usually must do what it says, even if you did not read it.

Look for the key terms. What is the total cost? How long does it last? What fees are there, such as late fees or fees to cancel early? Priya's phone deal had a $15 activation fee and a 36-month term. The *fine print* is the small text where these details often hide.

Before you sign, slow down. Take the papers home if you can. Ask what each fee is for. If a salesperson rushes you, that is a warning sign. In most states, anyone under 18 usually needs a parent or guardian to co-sign a big contract. Never sign a blank or unfinished form.

words.d: an agreement that the law can enforce
the small-print details in a contract, often about fees and rules
how long a contract or loan lasts

look.title: Priya's Checklist
look.text: Priya's phone offer: $0 down, $35 a month for 36 months, a $15 activation fee, and a required $70-a-month plan (example amounts).
look.prompt: What is the total cost of the phone itself, with the fee? What other question would you ask before signing?

check.q: Priya pays $35 a month for 36 months plus a $15 fee. What is the total for the phone?
A salesperson says, "Sign now, this deal ends in five minutes." What is the smart move?
choices: Slow down and read before signing
Sign a blank form to save time
check.why: Pressure is a warning sign. A good deal can wait for you to read it.

check.q: What is a contract?
choices: An agreement the law can enforce
check.why: Signing a contract creates legal duties.

Which card spends money directly from your bank account?
choices: A store gift card you were given
review.why: A debit card draws on your own account; a credit card is a loan.

review.q: A card has a 30% APR. About what is the monthly rate?
Which part counts most in a FICO credit score?
review.why: Payment history is about 35% of the score.

review.q: A loan is $250 a month for 60 months. What is the total paid?

review.why: Asking for a password with a prize is a classic phishing trick.
